target_name: Rancho San Francisco / Newhall Ranch, Los Angeles County
methodology: Ladera Ranch documentary half - hypothesis-neutral public-records screening. Soil status everywhere = UNSTUDIED. No claim of contamination.
earliest_imagery: Oldest topo: USGS Camulos 30-minute (later 15-minute) quadrangle, first edition dated August 1903 (1:62,500), which covers the western Santa Clara River valley / western Rancho San Francisco (the current Newhall Ranch Specific Plan land west of I-5 along the river toward the Ventura County line). The Newhall 15-minute quadrangle's earliest edition is 1933; downtown Newhall/Saugus (eastern communities) are on the Newhall sheet. So the topo floor for the WESTERN development footprint is 1903 (predates the dipping era) and for the EASTERN communities is 1933 (postdates it). Oldest aerial: the earliest aerial photography held for this area is the Fairchild Aerial Surveys (FAS) collection at UCSB, beginning ~1927; a labeled detail aerial of downtown Newhall dated 1930 is published on SCVHistory.com (LW3329), and 1945 Santa Clara River aerials appear in the CSUSB WRA collection. Both the 1903 Camulos topo and the ~1927 earliest aerial straddle the dipping window: the 1903 topo predates state-mandated arsenical dipping, while the earliest AERIAL (~1927) postdates dipping's ~1912 end by ~15 years - so any dip-era working facility would predate all available aerial photography and would be too small to resolve on the 1:62,500 topo.
review_start_year: The community's development carries an unusually LARGE and modern CEQA record - the opposite of most targets. The Newhall Ranch Specific Plan Final EIR (LA County, CEQAnet #1995011015) was certified with plan adoption in 2003; the overlapping Newhall Ranch Resource Management and Development Plan / Spineflower Conservation Plan (RMDP-SCP) Final EIS/EIR (CDFW + Army Corps) was completed June 2010; and tract-level Draft EIRs (Landmark Village 2006, Mission Village, Entrada) followed. These reviews included multiple ASTM Phase I Environmental Site Assessments (ENTRIX, Inc. technical report 2008; BA Environmental; Anacapa Geoservices) that expressly performed 'a review of historic aerial photographs, topographic maps, geologic maps' and site-specific historical review. The searchable text of the EIS/EIR Hazards section (4.17) confirms the Phase I aerial-photograph reviews were done but does NOT print the specific earliest aerial-photo YEAR each Phase I reached; given the regional archive, the earliest available aerial floor for this land is ~1927 (Fairchild/UCSB). Separately, in 2013 the LA Regional Water Quality Control Board required Newhall Land to sample agricultural-legacy soils for Organochlorine Pesticides (DDT and degradates) AND arsenic before development of historically-farmed areas - so arsenic and legacy agricultural chemistry ARE explicitly within the review's scope, though framed as generic agricultural/background chemistry, not as cattle-dip arsenic.
review_gap_years: HEADLINE: review_gap_years is approximately 15 years (earliest available aerial ~1927 minus dipping's ~1912 end). The Newhall reviews are extensive and modern, but their HISTORICAL AERIAL floor is bounded by what imagery exists: the oldest aerials of this land begin ~1927, so the entire active mandated-dipping window (roughly 1907-1912, and the broader tick-quarantine era back into the 1890s-1900s) sits BELOW the aerial-review floor by ~15 years or more. The Phase I ESAs also review topographic maps, and here the topo record does reach below the dipping era on the WESTERN footprint (Camulos 1903), but a plunge dip vat (~30-40 ft) is far below the resolution of a 1:62,500 topo, so the topo review cannot substitute for pre-1912 aerials. Two important nuances distinguish Newhall from a blind spot: (1) the exact earliest aerial YEAR reached by each Phase I is not printed in the searchable EIS/EIR text, so ~1927 is the archive-based floor, not a quoted review floor - if any Phase I happened to reach only ~1938/1947 imagery the gap would be ~26-35 years; and (2) the 2013 RWQCB workplan DID require arsenic + DDT soil testing of historically-agricultural parcels, so arsenic is not entirely unscreened here - but that screening targets 20th-century row-crop/orchard chemistry, not a specific pre-1912 dip facility, and no document ties arsenic sampling to cattle-dip history. Bottom line: no historical AERIAL review of this land reaches the pre-1912 mandated-dipping window; roughly 15+ years of the dipping era lie below the aerial floor.
dipping_records_summary: No cattle-dipping vat, dip charge, or arsenical-dip facility is tied to Rancho San Francisco / Newhall Ranch BY NAME in the materials searched (web search across CDNC framing, Chronicling America framing, SCVHistory.com, Wikipedia, San Diego History Center's California cattle-industry history, and general tick-eradication histories). Report this plainly: NONE BY NAME. Two direct CDNC full-text query attempts returned HTTP 403 and could not be read. What IS documented at the state/regional scale: California's law of 1907 compelled disinfection of tick-infested cattle by arsenical dip under the State Veterinarian, removing rancher discretion; the first officially permitted arsenical dip solution (white arsenic, soda, pine tar) dates to ~1910; DDT spraying replaced arsenical dipping ~1946. Rancho San Francisco / Newhall Ranch was a large, documented cattle-and-sheep operation (Ruth Waldo Newhall, 'Where Once Were Cattle'; a ~1940s sheep-flock photo, SCVHistory JN4902) on a ~46,460-acre grant, so the ranch clearly ran the kind of herds that the 1907 state mandate would have covered - but no facility has been located on this specific ranch. Absence of a named record is NOT evidence that no facility existed; several relevant historical sources are un-OCR'd scans or 403-blocked databases and were not fully searchable in this pass.
sampling_frame_plausibility: Plausible but unproven - do NOT assert a vat exists. Rancho San Francisco was one of Southern California's largest stock ranches: an 1839 Mexican grant (to the del Valle family) of ~48,000 acres, purchased by Henry Mayo Newhall in 1875 (~46,460 acres) and run as Newhall Land & Farming from 1883, carrying cattle and large sheep flocks well into the 20th century alongside irrigated farming (citrus, lima beans, row crops) in the Santa Clara River bottomlands. The terrain strongly supports intensive stock handling: the ranch straddles the perennial-to-seasonal Santa Clara River and its tributary canyons (San Martinez, Castaic, Potrero, Long Canyon), giving reliable water and natural corral topography - exactly where branding corrals and, during the 1907-1912 arsenical-dip mandate, a plunge vat would sit. A resident herd of this size in a state that legally compelled dipping in 1907 would have had to be dipped somewhere. HOWEVER, dipping was frequently centralized at shared inspection/community vats rather than one-per-ranch, and Los Angeles County was never one of the last-quarantined counties (by 1910 the remaining quarantine core was San Diego / Orange / Santa Barbara / part of San Luis Obispo), so LA-region herds may have been released from mandatory dipping earlier and a large ranch could have used an off-property or short-lived facility. No corral or vat has been located in imagery or records, and the modern Specific Plan footprint is only a fraction of the historic grant. Soil status remains UNSTUDIED.

findings.claim: The five named communities sit on the historic Rancho San Francisco, an 1839 Mexican land grant that Henry Mayo Newhall bought in 1875 (~46,460 acres) and ran as Newhall Land & Farming - a large documented cattle-and-sheep stock ranch.
findings.supporting: Newhall purchased the ~46,460-acre Rancho San Francisco in 1875 for ~$2/acre; the company (incorporated 1883) held ~143,000 acres across California; SCVHistory publishes Ruth Waldo Newhall's 'Where Once Were Cattle' and a ~1940s Newhall Ranch sheep-flock photo (JN4902), documenting active cattle and sheep operations.
findings.counter_evidence: The modern Newhall Ranch Specific Plan / Santa Clarita communities occupy only a portion of the historic grant; ranching intensity on the exact residential footprints (vs. the grant as a whole) is not individually documented, and the company pivoted toward oil and real estate by mid-century. Grant acreage figures vary by source (~46,460 to ~48,000 acres).
findings.citation: Wikipedia, 'Newhall Land and Farming Company'; ranchontheriver.com/history-of-newhall-ranch; SCVHistory.com JN4902 and ruth497.htm (B1/B2). Retrieved 2026-07-21.

findings.claim: California mandated arsenical cattle dipping under the State Veterinarian from 1907, using vats of white-arsenic solution, until DDT spraying replaced dipping ~1946 - establishing arsenical dipping as a statewide practice during ~1907-1912+.
findings.supporting: The 1907 California law compelled disinfection of tick-infested cattle by arsenical dip, removing rancher discretion; the first officially permitted arsenical solution (white arsenic, soda, pine tar) dates to ~1910; DDT replaced arsenic ~1946. General tick-eradication histories document 3,000-gallon arsenical vats and persistent residual arsenic at former vat sites.
findings.counter_evidence: This is state/regional context only - it does not place any dipping facility on Rancho San Francisco. By April 1910 the remaining hard-quarantine counties were San Diego, Orange, Santa Barbara and part of San Luis Obispo (not Los Angeles), so LA-region herds may have exited mandatory dipping earlier than the southern-coastal core.
findings.citation: San Diego History Center, 'California's Cattle-Range Industry, 1870-1912' (1965); tick-eradication histories (Medium/Koonce; USDA NAL) (B1/C). Retrieved 2026-07-21.

findings.claim: HEADLINE: The earliest historical AERIAL review floor for this land is ~1927, so the entire active mandated-dipping window (~1907-1912) sits ~15+ years below the aerial floor - review_gap_years approx. 15 years.
findings.supporting: The Newhall Phase I ESAs (ENTRIX 2008; BA Environmental; Anacapa) expressly reviewed 'historic aerial photographs, topographic maps, geologic maps'; the oldest aerials held for this area are the Fairchild (FAS) collection at UCSB beginning ~1927, with a published 1930 downtown-Newhall aerial (SCVHistory LW3329). 1927 minus dipping's ~1912 end = ~15 years below the aerial floor.
findings.counter_evidence: The searchable EIS/EIR Hazards text (4.17) confirms aerial reviews occurred but does NOT print the specific earliest aerial YEAR each Phase I reached, so ~1927 is an archive-based floor, not a quoted review floor - if a given Phase I reached only ~1938/1947 imagery the gap would be ~26-35 years. Conversely, the Phase I topographic-map review does reach 1903 (Camulos) on the western footprint, though a vat is below topo resolution.
findings.citation: RMDP-SCP Final EIS/EIR 4.17 (nrm.dfg.ca.gov DocumentID=21412, June 2010); UCSB Fairchild Aerial Surveys; SCVHistory LW3329 (A2/B1). Retrieved 2026-07-21.

findings.claim: The oldest topographic map covering the western development footprint is the 1903 USGS Camulos quadrangle, which predates the dipping era but is too coarse to depict a dip vat; the eastern communities' oldest topo is the 1933 Newhall quad.
findings.supporting: USGS/NGMDB and LAPL holdings list the Camulos 1:62,500 sheet from August 1903 covering the western Santa Clara River valley (Rancho San Francisco / current Newhall Ranch land), and the Newhall 15-minute quad's earliest edition as 1933.
findings.counter_evidence: At 1:62,500 a ~30-40 ft plunge vat and its corrals would not be depicted, so the 1903 topo cannot confirm or exclude a dip facility. Quadrangle coverage is split: downtown Newhall/Saugus/Canyon Country fall on the later (1933) Newhall sheet, not the 1903 Camulos sheet.
findings.citation: USGS topoView / NGMDB; LAPL 'Historical USGS Topographical Maps of Southern California'; TopoQuest Newhall cell (A2/B2). Retrieved 2026-07-21.

findings.claim: No cattle-dipping vat, arsenical-dip charge, or ranch working facility is tied to Rancho San Francisco / Newhall Ranch by name in the searchable materials.
findings.supporting: Targeted searches naming the ranch alongside 'dipping vat / arsenic / tick / State Veterinarian' returned only generic tick-eradication history and unrelated results; no named facility surfaced in web search, SCVHistory.com, Wikipedia, or land-grant histories.
findings.counter_evidence: This is 'the searchable materials do not identify X,' NOT 'X did not happen.' Two CDNC full-text queries returned HTTP 403 and could not be read; SCVHistory hosts many un-indexed scanned documents; a named record could exist in un-OCR'd archives, State Veterinarian annual reports, or LA County agricultural-commissioner records not surfaced here.
findings.citation: Web searches 2026-07-21 (see dead_ends); SCVHistory.com; general tick-eradication histories (B1/C for absence). Retrieved 2026-07-21.

findings.claim: Unlike a pure blind spot, the Newhall review DID require legacy-agricultural soil testing for DDT/organochlorine pesticides AND arsenic before developing historically-farmed parcels - though framed as generic agricultural/background chemistry, not cattle-dip arsenic.
findings.supporting: The LA Regional Water Quality Control Board's March 2013 'Soil Sampling for Pesticides' workplan for Newhall Land requires, in RMDP areas presently or historically used for agriculture, sampling for Organochlorine Pesticides (DDT and degradates, EPA 8081) and for arsenic (EPA 6000/7000), citing DTSC 2008 guidance; it notes arsenic 'is known to be relatively high in the soils of Southern California' and requires background samples.
findings.counter_evidence: This screening targets 20th-century row-crop/orchard pesticide legacy, NOT a pre-1912 cattle-dip facility; no document links the arsenic sampling to dipping history, and treating arsenic as regional background could mask a localized dip-vat signature. It also confirms arsenic testing was required, not that any specific parcel was found clean or contaminated - soil status remains UNSTUDIED.
findings.citation: LA RWQCB, 'Workplan Soil Sampling for Pesticides,' Newhall Land and Farming Co., March 2013 (waterboards.ca.gov/rwqcb4) (A1/A2). Retrieved 2026-07-21.

findings.claim: The ranch terrain makes an on-ranch working/dipping facility plausible during the 1907-1912 mandate, but no facility has been located and centralized/off-property vats are an equally plausible alternative.
findings.supporting: A large resident cattle/sheep herd on a ~46,460-acre grant, in a state that legally compelled dipping in 1907, plus reliable water and corral topography along the Santa Clara River and its canyons (Castaic, Potrero, San Martinez, Long Canyon), is a classic setting for corrals and a plunge vat.
findings.counter_evidence: Dipping was often centralized at shared inspection/community vats; Los Angeles County was not among the last hard-quarantine counties by 1910, so LA-region herds may have exited mandatory dipping earlier and a large operation could have used an off-property or short-lived facility. No corral/vat located in imagery or records; the modern footprint is a fraction of the grant. Soil status: UNSTUDIED.
findings.citation: Inference from 1907 CA dipping mandate + Rancho San Francisco extent/stock history + Santa Clara River hydrography (USGS). Model-based inference. Retrieved 2026-07-21.

findings.claim: No dip-era arsenic cleanup site on the Newhall Ranch footprint was identified in state environmental databases in this pass; the documented cleanup history is oil-field driven, and dip-era arsenic status is UNSTUDIED, not clean.
findings.supporting: The RMDP-SCP EIS/EIR Hazards section 4.17 details extensive remediation, but it is overwhelmingly OIL-FIELD legacy (Newhall-Potrero 1937, Castaic Junction 1950, Del Valle 1979 fields; tank batteries, sumps, DOGGR well abandonment) plus agricultural pesticide sampling - no cattle-dip arsenic site is described. GeoTracker/EnviroStor index cleanup sites but were not queried parcel-by-parcel here.
findings.counter_evidence: Absence of a dip-specific site is NOT a clean bill: these programs rarely investigate century-old dip-era arsenic absent a modern trigger, the databases were not searched with mapped bounding boxes, and the 2013 arsenic sampling treats arsenic as background rather than screening for a dip signature.
findings.citation: RMDP-SCP Final EIS/EIR 4.17 (nrm.dfg.ca.gov DocumentID=21412); GeoTracker (geotracker.waterboards.ca.gov); DTSC EnviroStor - screening-level, not exhaustive (A2). Retrieved 2026-07-21.
